steps.body: Five hikers carry 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 pounds: mean 6 (sum 30 ÷ 5) and median 6 — the summaries agree. Now a sixth hiker hauls **30** pounds. The sum leaps to 60, so the mean jumps to 60 ÷ 6 = **10** — bigger than five of the six packs! The median barely moves: the middle pair is 6 and 7, so it becomes **6.5**.

widget.prompt: Packs weigh 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 30 pounds. Compute the MEAN. (The sum is 60.)

commonErrors.feedback: 6 was the mean BEFORE the 30-pound pack joined. The new sum is 60 across 6 packs: 60 ÷ 6 = 10 — the outlier drags the mean up.
12 is 60 ÷ 5 — the count grew to SIX when the heavy pack joined. 60 ÷ 6 = 10.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Six packs now: 60 ÷ 6 = 10 pounds. One heavy pack lifted the mean above almost everyone.

explanationVariants: Sorted: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 30. Six values → middle pair 6 and 7 → median (6 + 7) ÷ 2 = 6.5. The 30 is just 'one value above the middle' — its SIZE never enters the calculation.
The median counts positions, not pounds: swap the 30 for a 9 or a 900 and the middle pair stays 6 and 7.

widget.prompt: Same packs — 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 30. What is the MEDIAN weight? (Decimals allowed.)

commonErrors.feedback: 10 is the MEAN — the summary the outlier dragged. The median averages the middle pair of the sorted list: (6 + 7) ÷ 2 = 6.5.
6 is only one of the two middle values. Six packs is an even count: median = (6 + 7) ÷ 2 = 6.5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Sorted, the middle pair is 6 and 7; the median is (6 + 7) ÷ 2 = 6.5 pounds.

hints: Even count — find the middle pair.

steps.body: That's the whole choice. The mean uses every value's **size**, so one extreme value — an **outlier** — can drag it far from the pack (6 → 10). The median uses only **position**, so it's **resistant**: it moved just half a step (6 → 6.5). Data with outliers or a strong skew? Report the **median**. Balanced, outlier-free data? The **mean** works — and the two will nearly agree anyway.

widget.prompt: Drag each statement to the summary it describes.

items.label: Uses the size of every single value
items.feedback: Every value's size flows into the sum — that's the mean's defining trait, and exactly why outliers can drag it.

items.label: Gets dragged toward an outlier
items.feedback: Dragging happens through the SUM — the outlier's whole size gets added in. That's the mean's weakness, not the median's.

items.label: Only cares which value stands in the middle
items.feedback: Position-not-size is the median's whole method — it's the middle of the sorted line-up.

items.label: Barely moves when one wild value joins
items.feedback: Resistance comes from ignoring size: a new value shifts the middle by at most one position. That's the median.

widget.missFeedback: Ask of each claim: does it depend on values' SIZES (mean territory) or only their POSITIONS (median territory)?
widget.successFeedback: Sorted — mean feels every pound; median only counts heads.

explanationVariants: The mansion is an outlier, and it drags the mean above what nearly every family actually pays — the median, resistant to the one extreme, describes the typical home honestly.
When one value dwarfs the rest, position beats size: report the median.

widget.prompt: A street has nine similar homes and one giant mansion. A report wants ONE number for the 'typical' home price. Which summary — and why?

options.label: Median — the mansion would drag the mean above almost every real home
options.feedback: Right — the median stays with the nine similar homes; the mean would chase the mansion.

options.label: Mean — it's more accurate because it uses every price
options.feedback: Using every price is exactly the vulnerability here: the mansion's full price inflates the sum, pushing the mean above what's typical. Choose the resistant median.

options.label: Either — mean and median always come out close
options.feedback: They agree on balanced data, but an outlier splits them apart — the pack data went mean 10 vs median 6.5. With a mansion in the mix, the choice matters.

hints: The mansion inflates the sum, and the sum feeds the mean.
The resistant one is the median.

explanationVariants: A mean far ABOVE the median is the signature of a high outlier (or a long high tail) — the mean got dragged up while the median held its ground.
When the two centers split, the mean points toward the extreme values; here it points high.

widget.prompt: A data set reports mean 42 and median 20. Without seeing the values, what's the most likely story?

options.label: Some very LARGE values are dragging the mean up past the middle
options.feedback: Exactly — a mean more than double the median almost always signals big values in a high tail pulling on the sum.

options.label: Some very SMALL values are dragging the mean down
options.feedback: Small extremes drag the mean BELOW the median — but this mean sits far above it, so the pull is coming from large values.

options.label: Someone must have miscalculated — mean and median can't differ
options.feedback: They differ whenever data is lopsided; the pack data legitimately gave mean 10 vs median 6.5. A big gap is information, not an error.

hints: Which direction did the mean move relative to the median?
Mean above median → big values pulling up.

explanationVariants: Without the 30: mean 6. With it: mean 10. The single outlier moved the mean by 10 − 6 = 4 pounds — while the median moved only 0.5.
Compare the two means you've already computed: 10 versus 6. The gap, 4, is the outlier's drag.

widget.prompt: The packs 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 have mean 6. Adding the 30-pound pack makes the mean 10. By how many pounds did the ONE outlier move the mean?

commonErrors.feedback: 0.5 is how far the MEDIAN moved (6 → 6.5) — the resistant summary. The mean went from 6 to 10: a 4-pound drag.
24 is the gap between the outlier (30) and the old mean (6) — not how far the mean itself moved. The mean went 6 → 10: a shift of 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The mean moved from 6 to 10; that's a shift of 10 − 6 = 4 pounds from a single value.

takeaways: The mean feels every value's size; one outlier can drag it far from the pack.
The median only counts positions, so it resists outliers — 6 → 6.5 while the mean leapt 6 → 10.
Outliers or skew → report the median; balanced data → the mean serves well.
steps.teaser: next chapter: centers answer 'where's the middle?' — now we measure how far the data SPREADS.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **The mean chases outliers; the median resists them.** Data 1, 2, 3 has mean 2 and median 2. Swap the 3 for a 30: the mean rockets to 11, but the sorted middle of 1, 2, 30 is still 2.

explanationVariants: Sorted, 1, 2, 30 still has 2 in the middle — the median ignores how big the 30 is.
The median counts positions: one value below 2, one above. Still 2.

widget.prompt: The data 1, 2, 3 becomes 1, 2, 30. What is the NEW median?

commonErrors.feedback: 11 is the new MEAN (33 ÷ 3) — the summary the outlier dragged. The middle of the sorted list 1, 2, 30 is still 2.
30 is the outlier itself, at the END of the sorted list. The middle value of 1, 2, 30 is 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Sort: 1, 2, 30. The middle value is 2 — the median didn't budge.
